title: Noradrenaline Neurons
intro: Noradrenaline (norepinephrine) in the cortex comes almost entirely from the locus coeruleus (LC), a tiny nucleus in the pons with a few thousand neurons in rodents and tens of thousands in humans. Their axons reach nearly every part of the brain. LC neurons switch between a tonic mode tied to arousal and a phasic mode of brief bursts to task-relevant or surprising events, and noradrenaline changes the gain of the neurons it reaches.

items: Firing: spontaneous pacemakers at about 0.5 to 5 Hz, faster in alert waking, slower in sleep and silent in REM sleep. Salient or unexpected stimuli evoke a brief phasic burst followed by a pause.

Tonic and phasic modes: in monkeys doing a detection task, moderate tonic firing with strong phasic responses to targets goes with good performance; high tonic firing with weak phasic responses goes with distractibility and exploration (Aston-Jones & Cohen 2005).

Coupling and modules: LC neurons are electrically coupled, which can synchronise them, but recent recordings show more modular structure than once thought, with groups that project to different targets and fire somewhat independently (Totah et al. 2018; Poe et al. 2020).

Receptors and effects: alpha-2 autoreceptors inhibit LC cells themselves; in targets, alpha-1, alpha-2 and beta receptors raise excitability, sharpen responses and enable plasticity. A common summary is that noradrenaline increases the gain of target neurons, making strong inputs stronger relative to weak ones.
Pupil: pupil diameter tracks LC activity closely enough to serve as a rough non-invasive readout (Joshi et al. 2016).
Gain modulation: Servan-Schreiber, Printz and Cohen (1990) modelled catecholamines as a change in the slope of the units' input-output function and showed this improves signal-to-noise in a network.

Adaptive gain theory: Aston-Jones and Cohen (2005) proposed that the LC switches between exploitation (phasic mode, gain boosted only for task-relevant events) and exploration (tonic mode, gain raised indiscriminately), driven by assessments of reward and cost in frontal cortex.

Coupled-oscillator LC model: Usher et al. (1999) showed that changing the electrotonic coupling between model LC neurons switches the population between phasic and tonic modes, and reproduced the link with performance.

Uncertainty: Yu and Dayan (2005) proposed that noradrenaline signals unexpected uncertainty (the world has changed) and acetylcholine expected uncertainty, so noradrenaline bursts should promote fast relearning. Bouret and Sara (2005) proposed a related 'network reset'.
Exploration temperature: in Doya's (2002) metalearning view, noradrenaline sets the randomness of action choice.

blocks.text: What this means for your SNN

items: Implement noradrenaline as a global multiplier on neuron gain (the slope of the f-I curve, or the inverse temperature of a winner-take-all) rather than as an extra input current.
A phasic burst at surprising events is a useful trigger for raising the learning rate or resetting a sequence memory; a tonic level sets how exploratory the system is.
In an HTM-style or cortical-column model, a surprise signal (many bursting columns) could drive an LC-like unit that in turn raises plasticity everywhere for a short time.
